chicken-or-turkey-and-noodles-with-tomat.title: Chicken or turkey and noodles with tomato-based sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of selected chicken or turkey fillet, boiled noodles, and a tomato‑based sauce made from ripe tomatoes, onion, garlic and aromatic herbs. It combines tender poultry protein, carbohydrate‑rich noodles and vitamin‑packed tomatoes for a balanced meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes used in the sauce are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
Chicken and turkey are among the most consumed meats worldwide due to their affordability and mild flavor.
The tradition of pairing noodles with tomato sauce dates back to Mediterranean cuisine, where pasta is often served with tomato‑based sauces.
Slow simmering of the sauce brings out the natural sweetness of tomatoes and reduces acidity.
The dish can be easily adapted to dietary needs by swapping regular noodles for whole‑grain or gluten‑free varieties.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Tomatoes supply vitamin C, vitamin K and potassium, while poultry adds iron and zinc.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (skinless)
items.content: Skinless fillets contain little saturated fat, making the dish suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Energy‑providing carbs
items.content: Noodles deliver quick‑release carbohydrates to sustain energy during active periods.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or turkey.

items.title: Sodium content in sauce
items.content: Prepared tomato sauces can be high in salt; monitor added sodium.

items.title: Glycemic index of noodles
items.content: Standard white noodles raise blood sugar quickly; whole‑grain options are preferable.

items.title: Undercooking risk
items.content: Insufficiently cooked poultry may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot: place noodles on a plate, top with a piece of chicken or turkey, drizzle with tomato sauce, and optionally garnish with fresh herbs or grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared meal in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat thoroughly to ensure poultry safety.

content.title: About
content.content: Lentils (Lens culinaris) are small, lens-shaped legume seeds that have been cultivated in the Near East for around 10,000 years. They come in many varieties, including brown, green, red, yellow, and black, and have an earthy flavor. Lentils are a staple in many cuisines and are used in soups, stews, salads, and dals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lentils are among the oldest cultivated crops in the world.
The word "lens" comes from the Latin word for lentil, because of the seed's shape.
Unlike many dried beans, lentils usually do not need to be soaked before cooking.
Red and yellow lentils cook quickly and break down into a creamy texture.
Lentils are a major source of protein in many vegetarian diets, especially in South Asia and the Middle East.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Lentils provide a good amount of protein for a plant food.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Lentils are high in fiber, which supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Provides folate and iron
items.content: These nutrients support cell function and oxygen transport.

items.title: Contains potassium and manganese
items.content: These minerals support normal blood pressure and metabolism.

items.title: Slow-digesting carbohydrates
items.content: Lentils have a relatively low glycemic index, so they raise blood sugar more slowly.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Lentils contain fermentable carbohydrates that may cause gas or bloating, especially in large amounts or when you are not used to them.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Lentil allergy is uncommon but can occur, and some people allergic to other legumes may also react.

items.title: Must be cooked
items.content: Raw or undercooked lentils can cause digestive upset, so cook them thoroughly.

items.title: Reduced iron absorption
items.content: Lentils contain compounds called phytates that can reduce mineral absorption. Eating them with vitamin C-rich foods can help the body absorb iron.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lentils can be rinsed and simmered until tender, then added to soups, stews, salads, and curries or served as a side dish. Red lentils are used for dals and purees, while green and brown lentils hold their shape for salads. Season them at the end of cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried lentils in an airtight container in a cool, dry place, where they keep for a year or longer. Cooked lentils should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to five days, or frozen for longer storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Wheat bran is the outer layer of the wheat grain obtained during milling. It is rich in dietary fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals. In Muffin, wheat bran, the bran is used as the main ingredient, giving the baked good a nutty aroma and boosting its nutritional value.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bran contains over 10 % protein and up to 30 % dietary fiber.
The fiber in bran helps regulate bowel movements and supports gut health.
Wheat bran is frequently used in diet and sports nutrition to increase satiety.
Bran contains phytoestrogens that may have a positive effect on hormonal balance.
It can be used as a natural thickener in sauces and soups.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion, promotes regular stools, and supports a healthy intestinal microbiome.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B2, B3 and folate are involved in energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Magnesium, iron and zinc in bran are important for muscle function, blood formation and immunity.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Bran raises blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for weight control and diabetes management.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The high fiber content slows stomach emptying, helping you feel full longer.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease may react to bran.

items.title: Excessive fiber intake
items.content: Too much bran can cause bloating, gas and abdominal discomfort.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Fiber may reduce the absorption of certain drugs; take medicines separately from bran.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wheat bran can be mixed into muffin, bread, pancake batters, added to yogurt, oatmeal, smoothies, or sprinkled over salads. It is also used as a coating for fish and meat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bran in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage keep it in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Boiled potato (NFS) is a selected variety of potato cooked by boiling in lightly salted water without added fats. It retains most of its nutrients, has a soft texture and a neutral flavor, making it a versatile base for many dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato is one of the most consumed vegetables worldwide.
Boiling preserves more vitamin C compared with frying, though some is lost in the water.
NFS (Non‑Fried Standard) indicates a product without added fats and minimal processing.
Boiled potato is easy to digest and often recommended in dietetic nutrition.
There are over 4,000 potato varieties, but only a small fraction are suitable for boiling.

items.title: Rich in carbohydrates
items.content: Potato provides complex carbohydrates that deliver a steady source of energy.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Boiled potato retains vitamin C, which supports immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: The skin and flesh contain fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fats makes boiled potato suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Boiled potato can raise blood sugar quickly, which is important for people with diabetes.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to potato.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding salt to the cooking water increases sodium levels; those with hypertension should monitor salt intake.

items.title: Potential acrylamide formation
items.content: Prolonged storage and reheating can lead to small amounts of acrylamide, a possible carcinogen.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boiled potato can be eaten on its own, added to salads, soups, mashed, or used as a base for casseroles. It is convenient to cut into cubes, slices, or mash. For extra flavor, season with herbs, a drizzle of olive oil, or a light yogurt dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store boiled potato in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. Longer storage may cause it to become dry and lose flavor. Before eating, check for any off‑odors or signs of mold.

rice-white-with-other-vegetables-fat-add.title: White Rice with Vegetables and Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: White rice cooked with a mix of vegetables (carrot, peas, corn) and a touch of vegetable oil is a nutritious dish commonly found in Asian and Mediterranean cuisines. The rice provides carbohydrate‑based energy, the vegetables add vitamins and fiber, and the added fat enhances flavor and aids the absorption of fat‑soluble nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice loses many of its natural vitamins and minerals during polishing, so it is often enriched with iron and B‑vitamins.
Combining rice with vegetables increases the overall fiber content, supporting better digestion.
A small amount of vegetable oil (e.g., olive oil) improves taste and helps absorb carotenoids from the vegetables.
Traditionally the dish is steamed or simmered to keep vegetables crisp and rice fluffy.
In many cultures the rice‑vegetable mix is served as a side dish alongside meat or fish.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice delivers quick‑acting carbohydrates that fuel physical and mental activities.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Vegetables contribute vitamin A, vitamin C, folate, and potassium, supporting immunity and heart health.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Vegetable oil, especially olive oil, provides monounsaturated fatty acids beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The added vegetables raise the fiber content, promoting regular bowel movements and satiety.

items.title: Improved nutrient absorption
items.content: Fats aid the body in absorbing carotenoids and vitamin K present in the vegetables.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes in people with diabetes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding soy sauce or extra salt can make the dish too salty, which is undesirable for those with hypertension.

items.title: Allergy to certain oils
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to specific vegetable oils.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: The combination of rice, oil, and vegetables can increase the calorie count, so portion control is important for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main meal or as a side to meat, fish, or tofu. It reheats well in the microwave or on a skillet; add a splash of water to prevent drying out.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked rice with vegetables in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for 1‑2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before eating.

soft-drink-fruit-flavored-caffeine-conta.title: Soft Drink, Fruit Flavored, Caffeine Containing

content.title: About
content.content: A fruit‑flavored soft drink with caffeine is a refreshing non‑alcoholic beverage that combines natural fruit extracts, sugar (or sweeteners) and caffeine for a mild stimulant effect. These drinks are popular as a lighter‑tasting alternative to colas and energy drinks, offering a crisp fruit profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fruit flavorings are often derived from real juices but may be enhanced with synthetic compounds for consistency.
Caffeine levels typically range from 30 to 80 mg per 330 ml can, lower than a standard cup of coffee.
The first fruit‑flavored carbonated drink appeared in the late 19th century during experiments with flavored soda water.
In some countries these beverages are classified as “energy drinks,” requiring special labeling.
Packaging usually features bright colors to highlight the fruity character.

items.title: Improved focus
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, enhancing alertness and reaction time.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Carbonated water contributes to daily fluid intake when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Vitamin contribution
items.content: Fruit extracts can provide small amounts of vitamin C and antioxidants.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of sugar (or sweeteners) and caffeine delivers a quick rise in energy levels.

items.title: Mood uplift
items.content: Sweet taste and pleasant aroma may temporarily improve mood.

items.title: Excess caffeine
items.content: Too much caffeine can cause anxiety, insomnia, and rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: High sugar intake raises the risk of cavities, weight gain, and metabolic disorders.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature of carbonated drinks can irritate the stomach lining and erode tooth enamel.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some flavoring agents may trigger individual sensitivities.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Serve the fruit‑flavored soft drink chilled, preferably in moderate amounts (no more than 1‑2 cans per day). It can be used as a base for cocktails, mixed with juices, or incorporated into recipes such as marinades.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the beverage in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, store it in the refrigerator and consume within 3‑5 days to maintain carbonation and flavor.
